rewritten_text:
Without pausing to think, and barely aware of her own feelings, Elizabeth finished the letter and immediately snatched up the other. She opened it in the greatest impatience and read the following; it had been written a day after the first letter was completed.

“By now, my dearest sister, you will have received my hurried letter. I hope this one makes more sense, but although I am not short of time, my thoughts are so confused that I cannot promise to be coherent. Dearest Lizzy, I hardly know what to write, but I have bad news that cannot wait. However unwise a marriage between Mr. Wickham and our poor Lydia would be, we are now desperate to know that it has happened, because there is all too much reason to fear they have not gone to Scotland. Colonel Forster arrived yesterday, having left Brighton the previous day, only a few hours after the express messenger. Lydia’s brief note to Mrs. F. led them to believe they were going to Gretna Green. But Denny let slip that he thought W. had never intended to go there, or to marry Lydia at all. This was repeated to Colonel F., who became alarmed at once and left B. to follow their route. He traced them easily as far as Clapham, but no farther. On entering the town, they changed into a hired coach and dismissed the chaise that had brought them from Epsom. All anyone knows after that is that they were seen continuing along the London road. I do not know what to think. After making every possible inquiry on that side of London, Colonel F. continued into Hertfordshire, anxiously asking again at all the tollgates and at the inns in Barnet and Hatfield. He had no success: no one had seen such people pass through. With the kindest concern, he came on to Longbourn and told us his fears in a way that showed the goodness of his heart. I feel deeply sorry for him and Mrs. F., but nobody can blame them. Our distress, my dear Lizzy, is very great. Father and Mother believe the worst, but I cannot think so badly of him. Many circumstances might make a private marriage in London more convenient than following their original plan. And even if he could intend such a thing against a young woman of Lydia’s family connections, which seems unlikely, can I believe she would forget every principle? Impossible! Sadly, however, Colonel F. does not seem willing to rely on their marrying. When I expressed my hopes, he shook his head and said he feared W. was not a trustworthy man.

The day went by in much the same manner as the preceding one. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley passed several morning hours with the invalid, whose recovery continued, though slowly; and that evening Elizabeth joined the company in the drawing-room. The loo table, however, was not brought out. Mr. Darcy was occupied in writing, while Miss Bingley sat beside him, following the progress of his letter and frequently distracting him with messages for his sister. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Bingley played piquet, with Mrs. Hurst watching their game.

Elizabeth picked up some needlework and found ample amusement in listening to the exchange between Darcy and his companion. The lady’s unceasing compliments upon his handwriting, the regularity of his lines, or the length of his letter, together with the entire indifference that greeted her praise, made a curious conversation, perfectly consistent with Elizabeth’s judgment of them both.

“What pleasure such a letter will give Miss Darcy!”

He offered no reply.

“You write extraordinarily quickly.”

“You are mistaken; I write rather slowly.”

“What a quantity of letters you must need to write in a year! Business letters as well! I should find them so hateful!”

“Then it is fortunate that the task belongs to me rather than you.”

“Do tell your sister how much I wish to see her.”

“At your request, I have already told her once.”

“I fear your pen does not please you. Allow me to mend it. I am remarkably good at mending pens.”

“Thank you, but I invariably mend my own.”

“How do you manage to make your writing so even?”

He said nothing.

“Tell your sister how pleased I am to hear of her progress on the harp, and do say that her lovely little design for a table has quite enchanted me. I consider it infinitely better than Miss Grantley’s.”

“May I postpone your enchantment until my next letter? There is not enough room at present to represent it properly.”

“Oh, it is no matter. I shall see her in January. But are your letters to her always so delightfully long, Mr. Darcy?”

“They are usually long; whether they are always delightful must be left to others to decide.”

“My rule is that anyone who can compose a long letter easily cannot write badly.”

“That will not serve as a compliment to Darcy, Caroline,” her brother exclaimed, “for he does not write easily. He takes far too much trouble finding words of four syllables. Do you not, Darcy?”

“My manner of writing differs considerably from yours.”

“Oh,” exclaimed Miss Bingley, “Charles writes as carelessly as anyone possibly could.

I thanked him and apologised. “Not at all,” he replied, and continued.

“Miss Havisham had now inherited a fortune, and naturally people considered her a very desirable bride. Her half-brother once again had plenty of money, but his debts and fresh foolishness soon swallowed it up just as recklessly as before. He and his sister quarrelled even more bitterly than he and his father had. People suspect that he deeply hated her because he believed she had helped turn their father against him. Now we reach the cruel part of the story—I must just pause, my dear Handel, to point out that a dinner napkin will not fit inside a drinking glass.”

I cannot possibly explain why I was trying to stuff mine into my glass. I only know that I discovered myself working very hard to squeeze it in, with a determination that deserved a better purpose. Once again I thanked him and apologised. Once again he said, with the greatest cheerfulness, “Not at all, I assure you!” and went on.

“A certain man appeared—at the races, or a public dance, or wherever you please—and began courting Miss Havisham. I never saw him, since all this happened twenty-five years ago, before either of us was born, Handel. But I have heard my father say he was a flashy man, well suited to what he intended. My father insists, however, that nobody who was neither ignorant nor prejudiced could have mistaken him for a gentleman. My father firmly believes that, since the beginning of the world, no man who lacked a gentleman’s true character ever had a gentleman’s true manners. He says you cannot hide the grain of wood with varnish; the more coats you apply, the more clearly the grain shows through. Well, this man pursued Miss Havisham eagerly and declared himself utterly devoted to her. I believe she had never been particularly open to love before, but every bit of tenderness in her came out then, and she loved him passionately. There is no doubt she worshipped him. He exploited her affection so methodically that he obtained enormous sums of money from her. He also persuaded her to buy her brother’s share in the brewery at an enormous price—a share their father had weakly left him. His excuse was that, once they married, he must own and manage the whole business. Your guardian was not advising Miss Havisham at that time, and she was too proud and too deeply in love to accept advice from anyone.”
